sections.body_en:
A Jew who bought or received from a non-Jew a food vessel made of metal or glass is commanded to immerse it in a mikveh to purify it, like a convert who immerses at the time of his conversion. Even if the vessel was made in a factory belonging to a Jew, if a non-Jew bought it, the vessel became his, and a Jew who buys the vessel from him must immerse it. If the non-Jew used the vessel with forbidden foods, it must first be kashered in the manner of its use, in order to remove from it the tastes of the prohibition that were absorbed in it or stuck to it, and afterwards it is immersed for the sake of purification.

These two mitzvot, kashering vessels and immersing them, we learned from what is stated in the Torah about the spoils that the Israelites took from the Midianites (Bamidbar 31:21-23): "This is the statute of the Torah which the Lord commanded Moshe. Only the gold, and the silver, the copper, the iron, the tin and the lead – everything that may go through fire you shall pass through fire and it shall be clean; nevertheless it shall be purified with the water of sprinkling (mei nidda); and all that may not go through fire you shall pass through water." Passing through fire or boiling water is for vessels in which forbidden foods were cooked or roasted, and just as they were used for something forbidden, so must they be kashered (below 32:1). In addition it is stated: "and it shall be clean; nevertheless it shall be purified with mei nidda," to teach us that the vessel must also be purified by immersing it in a mikveh in which a nidda immerses for her purification (Avoda Zara 75b; Ramban). There is no connection between the two mitzvot; rather, if the non-Jew used the vessel for forbidden foods, it must be both kashered and immersed, and if he did not use it for forbidden foods, it need only be immersed.

The aim of the mitzva of immersion is to elevate the vessel from the level of a vessel intended for ordinary eating, which is accompanied by desire and human weaknesses, to the level of a vessel intended for preparing foods through which Jews can connect to the values of the Torah. This mitzva is one of a system of mitzvot intended to distinguish the eating of Jews as eating that contains faith, holiness and blessing. Therefore, Jews were commanded to recite blessings before and after eating, not to eat forbidden foods that express other aims, to separate gifts from the foods for the kohanim, the Levites and the poor, and to bring some of them up to Jerusalem and eat them there in holiness. The mitzva of immersing vessels is intended to purify the vessel from the impurity that clings to ordinary eating, which is meant to sustain a person during his days in this world, so that through his eating a Jew can connect more to eternal values and the vision of repairing the world (tikkun olam).

sections.title_en: Vessels of Metal, Glass and Other Materials
sections.body_en:
The vessels that require immersion by Torah law are vessels made of metal, such as gold, silver, copper, iron, tin and lead, which the Torah enumerated, and all other metals are included in this. The Sages added and enacted that glass vessels must also be immersed, because of the similarity of glass to metal: just as metal can be melted down and new vessels made from it, so glass vessels can be melted down and new vessels made from them (Avoda Zara 75b).

But vessels made of other materials, such as earthenware, porcelain, ceramic, stone, wood and plastic of its various kinds, are exempt from immersion. And although plastic vessels can be melted down like glass, we should not, on our own judgment, extend the enactment to vessels that resemble glass.

Metal vessels coated with various coatings, such as Teflon, enamel or ceramic coating, require immersion with a blessing, for they are essentially metal. The same applies to Corelle plates, which are essentially glass.

China vessels, that is, vessels that are essentially earthenware coated with a very thin glassy glaze, are exempt from immersion, since the glaze is subordinate to the earthenware (Knesset Ha-gedola, Ḥida, She'ilat Ya'avetz and Yad Efrayim).1

A metal pot with plastic handles, and likewise a knife whose handle is wood, require immersion, and the entire vessel must be immersed, including the part made of material that does not require immersion. This is the rule: whenever the main component of the vessel, which comes into contact with the food, is made of metal or glass, the entire vessel requires immersion.

notes_en.en:
The opinion of the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim is that the mitzva of immersing metal vessels is by Torah law; so wrote Rashi, Rabbeinu Tam, Ra'avad, Rashba, Ra'ah, Rabbeinu Yeḥiel of Paris, Semag, Rosh, Semak, Ritva, and others. And some say that it is rabbinic: Tosafot Rid, Rashbatz and others, and so many understood the opinion of the Rambam (see Tevilat Kelim, Introduction 3). Since according to most poskim the mitzva is by Torah law, in a case of doubt we are stringent to immerse without a blessing, and we do not rely on a minor who testified about himself that he immersed a vessel (SA 120:14; below note 6).
Some hold that plastic and nylon vessels require immersion without a blessing, since they too can be melted down like glass vessels (Minḥat Yitzḥak 3:76-78). However, according to the overwhelming majority of Aḥaronim, since the obligation for glass vessels is a rabbinic enactment, it should not be extended to what they did not enact (Melamed Le-ho'il YD 49; Ḥelkat Ya'akov 2:163:2; Yabi'a Omer 4, YD 8; Tzitz Eliezer 7:37; Rav Yosef Eliyahu Henkin). It is worth noting that the similarity between glass and metal vessels is also great, for they are strong and hard, and there are kinds in which one can even cook, whereas as of today one generally does not cook in plastic vessels. And since this is the opinion of most poskim, and the discussion concerns a rabbinic mitzva, the halakha follows the lenient authorities.
An earthenware vessel that is coated with glass inside and out requires immersion with a blessing (based on SA and Rema 120:1; Pri Ḥadash). Apparently, the intent is a thick coating and not a very thin one as with china and porcelain vessels, which most poskim agree are exempt from immersion (Knesset Ha-gedola; She'ilat Ya'avetz; Ḥida, Shiyurei Berakha 120:3; Yad Efrayim 1; Shulḥan Gavoha 5; Erekh Ha-shulḥan 3. According to the Ben Ish Ḥai, Year 2, Matot 7, one should be stringent and immerse them without a blessing, and so wrote Ḥut Ha-shani and Tevilat Kelim 11:170).

sections.title_en: Eating Vessels Are Subject to the Mitzva
sections.body_en:
The vessels included in the mitzva are vessels from which one eats and drinks, such as plates, cups and cutlery, as well as serving vessels such as bowls, pitchers and trays. Likewise vessels in which food is prepared, such as pots and their lids, frying pans, baking pans, skewers, and grills for roasting. But a trivet does not require immersion, since foods are not placed on it, only pots. And even though eggplants are sometimes roasted on it, since its main use is for pots, it does not require immersion (SA 120:4).

Likewise, one must immerse a grater, a peeler, a garlic and spice grinder, an egg slicer, a tea strainer and a nutcracker, since they come into direct contact with the food. But a corkscrew and a can opener, which are not intended to come into contact with the food, are exempt from immersion.

Vessels that come into contact with food but are intended for its preparation in the stages preceding the stage in which it is prepared for eating, such as slaughtering knives and vessels used for preparing dough, are exempt from immersion. This is the rule: all vessels that come into direct contact with the food when it is fit to eat require immersion (SA 120:4-5).2

Vessels intended for storing foods in the kitchen, such as a jar for sugar or coffee, require immersion. But if wrapped foods are placed in them, such as wrapped candies or tea bags, they do not require immersion.

Vessels intended for storing foods in a storeroom, since one does not usually take food from them to eat immediately, are exempt from immersion. Disposable vessels are exempt from immersion (below, halakha 9). The law of electrical appliances will be explained below (halakha 10).3

notes_en.en:
A pot lid requires immersion like the pot, since it is part of the pot, and in addition it holds the condensation, which is also part of the cooked food (Rema 120:5; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 32). For immersing both, one recites the blessing "al tevilat kelim." A baking pan that one usually bakes in with baking paper requires immersion, since the baking paper is subordinate to the pan (Minḥat Shlomo vol. 2, 66:5).
A slaughtering knife, according to the Mordekhai, is exempt from immersion. And so wrote the Issur Ve-heter He-arokh 58:84-85 in the name of the Ra'avya, and so he wrote there regarding a tool used to perforate matza dough. And so it was ruled in SA 120:5. The Rema wrote regarding a slaughtering knife, based on the Maharash and Sefer Tashbetz Katan 326, that some disagree and it is good to immerse it without a blessing. The Aḥaronim disagreed about his opinion: some say that in his opinion even a vessel in which food is prepared before it is fit to eat requires immersion without a blessing (Taz 7; Gra), and some say that a slaughtering knife requires immersion without a blessing because it is sometimes also used for ready-to-eat food, but a vessel intended for use only before the food is fit to eat, such as a kneading vessel, is exempt even according to the Rema (Shakh 11; Knesset Ha-gedola). And so one should rule, combining the opinion of the SA and those who follow his approach, who exempt a slaughtering knife even if it is sometimes used for ready-to-eat food (and so wrote Rav Shlomo Kluger, Responsa Tuv Ta'am Va-da'at, Mahadura Gimel 2:22); and one who wishes to be stringent should immerse it without a blessing.
A nutcracker and a peeler: according to Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach in Minḥat Shlomo vol. 2, 66:6, they require immersion with a blessing. The Shevet Ha-levi 6:245 wrote not to recite the blessing because it is similar to a can opener, and in Halikhot Olam vol. 7, p. 267, he wrote that it is exempt from immersion but it is good to immerse it without a blessing. It appears that the halakha follows Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, for these are vessels that handle the food itself, and not an external packaging that people made for the food. And since immediately after the cracking or peeling the food is eaten, it requires immersion with a blessing.

Storage vessels that are not brought to the table: Responsa Beit Yehuda (Ayash) YD 52 wrote that they are exempt from immersion because one does not eat from them, and some took his words into account and ruled to immerse without a blessing, and so wrote Tevilat Kelim 11:16. However, the Beit David YD 62 ruled that they require immersion with a blessing, and the Shiyurei Berakha 120:1 cited him and ruled like him, and so wrote the Ben Ish Ḥai, Year 2, Matot 5. It appears in practice that storage vessels intended for a storeroom are exempt from immersion, but kitchen storage vessels, from which food is sometimes taken directly for eating, such as sugar and coffee, are considered eating vessels and require immersion with a blessing.
Some say that even with a vessel not intended for food, such as a scribe's knife or a 'Leatherman' pocketknife, it is forbidden to use it occasionally for food without immersion (Issur Ve-heter He-arokh 58:85; Rema 120:8). However, according to most poskim, if most of its use is not for food, it does not require immersion (Pri Ḥadash 120:19, 22; Pitḥei Teshuva 6; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 40; Ben Ish Ḥai, Year 2, Matot 11). And the Pri To'ar 11 wrote that we are not concerned about its minority use when the main purpose of the vessel does not require immersion. I did not write that it is good to be stringent in accordance with its minority use, both because one should follow the majority of poskim and because their reasoning is convincing. In addition, the Issur Ve-heter He-arokh 58:85 wrote that when they do not require immersion, it is preferable not to immerse them without a blessing, lest one forget and recite the blessing.

sections.body_en:
The immersion of the vessel must be done in a kosher mikveh, in which the quantity of water is at least forty se'a, the amount in which an average person can immerse his whole body at once – one amma by one amma by three ammot.4

The mikveh is kosher provided that its water is living water flowing from a spring, or rainwater that collected in the sea or in a mikveh. But if its water was brought in vessels or through pipes, it is not kosher for a mikveh.

The fundamental rule of immersion is that the entire vessel must be in the water, without anything interposing between the vessel and the water of the mikveh. Therefore, one who immerses half of the vessel and afterwards its other half, his immersion is invalid, since the whole vessel was not in the water at once. The handle of the vessel is also included in the vessel, and therefore if part of it remains outside the water, the immersion is invalid (SA 120:12; Pitḥei Teshuva 3). Likewise, one must check that nothing at all, and no dirt, is stuck to the vessel, whether inside or outside, for anything that people usually take care to remove from the vessel interposes between the vessel and the water and invalidates the immersion (SA 120:13). Likewise, one must remove the price label and the glue under it, since people usually remove them before use. However, tiny remnants of glue or dirt that people do not usually take care to remove, if the owner of the vessel also does not usually take care about them, do not interpose. When an attractive manufacturer's label is stuck to the vessel, which many people usually leave on during use, and the owner of the vessel also wants it, it is considered part of the vessel and need not be removed before the immersion.

When, in addition to immersion, the vessel must also be kashered because non-kosher food was cooked in it, one must kasher it first and complete its purification with the immersion. After the fact, if it was immersed first, as long as nothing interposing between the vessel and the water was stuck to the vessel, its immersion is valid (SA 121:2).

A vessel composed of several parts may be immersed while assembled, even though the water does not enter the place where the parts are joined, since the immersion is done in the manner in which the vessel is used (Har Tzvi YD 108). When immersing a vessel with a narrow opening, such as a bottle, one must make sure that the water fills it completely, so that all of it, outside and inside, comes into full contact with the water.

After inserting the vessel into the mikveh water, one must loosen one's grip on it for a split second, so that the mikveh water enters between the hand and the vessel; otherwise, the hand holding the vessel will interpose between the water and the vessel. One who is afraid to let go of the vessel lest it fall and break should first wet his hand in the mikveh water, and while it is still in the mikveh, transfer the vessel to it from his other hand. In this way he can hold the vessel firmly, for since his hand is already wet with the mikveh water, the mikveh water comes into contact with the vessel even where he is holding it (Rema 120:2). Another solution is to put the vessel in a basket, so that there is no concern that the vessel will fall and break, and there is also no interposition between the basket and the vessel, since they are not tight against each other. If one put several vessels in the basket, one should shake them in the mikveh water to ensure that the water enters between them.5

notes_en.en: The size of a mikveh, forty se'a, is 288 liters, and ab initio the custom is that it should contain close to a thousand liters. In a spring, according to several Rishonim (Or Zaru'a, Tur, Agur, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam and Rashbatz), one may immerse even in less than forty se'a, as with the immersion of vessels from corpse impurity. However, according to Rabbeinu Tam and the Semak, and so it was ruled in SA 120:1, even in a spring forty se'a are required (see Arukh Ha-shulḥan 120:10, who was lenient like the Tur in a pressing situation).

Mishna Mikva'ot 8:5: "One who holds a person or vessels and immerses them – they are impure… Rabbi Shimon says: he should loosen [his grip], so that the water may come into them." Many of the Rishonim ruled stringently like the first Tanna that holding interposes, and as the Rambam explained, because of the concern that one might hold tightly and not loosen (Hilkhot Mikva'ot 2:11). And so wrote the Ramban, Ra'ah, Baḥ and Shakh 120:6. On the other hand, the Behag, Tur, Rashba and SA 120:2, Taz and Gra ruled leniently like Rabbi Shimon that one may hold loosely. Ab initio one should satisfy all opinions. The SA 120:2 wrote: "And if he moistened his hand in water first, there is no concern," that is, he may hold the vessel neither loosely nor tightly; and so wrote the Taz, Pri Ḥadash, Pri To'ar, Zivḥei Tzedek and others. Wetting the hand may be done with any water whatsoever. The Rema wrote that one should wet the hand in the mikveh water, and in this way one may hold the vessel tightly. Simply understood, the intent is that one inserts the hand into the mikveh water and does not take it out, and then all the moisture on the hand is considered part of the mikveh. And so wrote the Levush, Mateh Yehonatan, Arugot Ha-bosem and others.

sections.title_en: The Blessing, and Immersion by a Minor or a Non-Jew
sections.body_en:
Before immersing the vessels, one recites the blessing: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the immersion of vessels (al tevilat kelim)." If it is one vessel: "concerning the immersion of a vessel (al tevilat keli)" (SA YD 120:3).

A boy or girl who has not reached the age of obligation in mitzvot may immerse vessels and recite the blessing before their immersion, but they are not qualified to testify that they immersed the vessels properly. Therefore, only if an adult testifies that they immersed the vessels properly may the vessels they immersed be used. If a child was sent to immerse vessels and no adult was there to testify about it, the vessels he immersed must be immersed again with a blessing. And if the child is known to be reliable, the vessels he immersed must be immersed again without a blessing (SA 120:14).6

A non-Jew is also qualified to immerse vessels, but since he is not obligated in the mitzva, he cannot testify to its fulfillment, nor can he recite a blessing over its fulfillment. Therefore, one should not send a non-Jew to immerse the vessels. But a Jew may be assisted by a non-Jew in such a way that the Jew recites the blessing and immerses the first vessel, and afterwards asks the non-Jew to immerse the remaining vessels while the Jew watches and sees him immersing all the vessels (SA 120:15).

In most mikva'ot a special mikveh is prepared for immersing vessels, and then one must be careful to immerse the vessels specifically in it: first, to avoid the concern that one of the vessels might fall into the mikveh and injure the feet of those immersing; second, because it is more proper to recite the blessing close to it.7

notes_en.en:
As a rule, we do not rely on the testimony of a child regarding a Torah mitzva, and since the mitzva of immersing vessels is by Torah law, we do not rely on him. Accordingly, Rabbi Akiva Eiger wrote that seemingly one could rely on him regarding the immersion of glass vessels, whose mitzva is rabbinic. However, according to Tosafot (Eruvin 31b, s.v. "Kan"), only regarding something that belongs to the minor can one rely on him in a rabbinic law, but not when he is sent to immerse his parents' vessel. End of quote. And according to the Pri Megadim (OḤ 451, Mishbetzot Zahav 10), even regarding glass one should not be lenient, since they have a presumptive status of being forbidden.
Just as the immersion of a nidda does not require intention, so too the immersion of a vessel does not require intention; thus, if the vessel fell into the mikveh unintentionally and a Jew saw it, the vessel is purified (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 120:12).

In the past it was forbidden to recite blessings in mikva'ot, because they were filthy, since people washed in the same room and there were no pipes to drain away the dirt as in our day. Therefore, despite the distance, the custom was to recite the blessing outside the mikveh, and without an interruption of speech they would enter and perform the immersion (see MB 84:4; Yabi'a Omer vol. 2, YD 14). But today mikva'ot are clean, and therefore, although as a rule one may not say anything holy in a place where people are usually undressed (SA OḤ 84:1), the blessing over immersion, whose place is there, may be recited. But it is clear that it is more proper to recite the blessing next to the vessel mikveh that is outside.

sections.title_en: The Transfer from a Non-Jew to a Jew That Creates the Obligation of Immersion
sections.body_en:
A vessel that a Jew bought from a non-Jew, as long as he does not intend to use it for eating purposes, need not be immersed. Therefore, a Jewish merchant who bought eating vessels from a non-Jew for commercial purposes need not immerse them, but a Jew who buys them from him in order to use them will be obligated to immerse them. Likewise, the merchant himself, if he decides to take a vessel from his merchandise stock for his own use, will be obligated to immerse it.

A vessel that was produced in a factory belonging to a Jew and sold to a non-Jewish wholesaler, who sold it to a Jewish merchant, and a Jew bought it for eating purposes, must be immersed, since there was a time when the vessel was owned by a non-Jew (SA 120:11).

A vessel produced in a factory belonging to a Jew, even if all the workers in the factory are non-Jews, is exempt from immersion, since the workers are hired employees and the vessels belong to the Jew alone (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 120:58; Darkhei Teshuva 81).

A vessel produced in a factory jointly owned by a Jew and a non-Jew: since the non-Jew is also a partner in the ownership of the factory, a Jew who buys a vessel from this factory must immerse it with a blessing. Therefore, one who buys a vessel that was produced abroad must immerse it with a blessing, since the overwhelming majority of factories abroad belong to non-Jews, or at least non-Jews are partners in their ownership. But one who buys in Israel, in a Jew's store, a vessel produced in a Jew's factory, need not immerse the vessel, because without a special reason, there is no concern that perhaps at one of the stages the vessel belonged to a non-Jewish merchant. It is proper for store owners to clarify carefully the origin of the vessels they sell, so that they can inform buyers whether they must immerse the vessels with a blessing, and without this they do not serve their customers properly.8

A vessel that a Jew and a non-Jew bought in partnership from a non-Jew does not require immersion, since it did not pass entirely into the Jew's possession. If the Jew buys the non-Jew's share, he will be obligated to immerse the vessel with a blessing (Rema 120:11; Shakh 26). Eating vessels bought by the IDF, the Israel Police and other bodies belonging to the State of Israel require immersion with a blessing; and although there are non-Jewish citizens in the State with full civil rights, since the State of Israel is defined as a Jewish state, the vessels require immersion.

A convert need not immerse his vessels, because when he becomes a Jew, the vessels in his possession are also purified with him.9

notes_en.en:
The Shakh 120:26, Pri Ḥadash 35 and other Aḥaronim wrote that a vessel in which a Jew and a non-Jew were partners, and the Jew bought the non-Jew's share, must be immersed. Similarly, if the factory originally belonged to a Jew and a non-Jew, a vessel bought from it requires immersion (Arugot Ha-bosem YD 122:5, and others). When the factory is abroad, there is no need to be concerned about the slim chance that the factory belongs entirely to a Jew and that all the intermediaries along the way were Jews, and therefore vessels produced abroad must be immersed with a blessing (see Ḥelkat Binyamin 120:2). A Jew who gave a non-Jew metal so that the non-Jew would make a vessel from it for a contract payment: according to the Rosh and SA 120:10, it does not require immersion. And some say that it requires immersion (because a craftsman acquires ownership through the improvement of the vessel), and the Rema wrote to immerse it without a blessing. A Jew who gave a vessel as a pledge to a non-Jew, when it is returned, it does not require immersion, for it was not yet in the non-Jew's ownership (SA 120:11). One should not sell ḥametz vessels before Pesaḥ, so that it will not be necessary to immerse them afterwards (Peninei Halakha: Pesaḥ 6, note 6).
A Jewish factory that issued shares, some of which were bought by non-Jews: its vessels do not require immersion, since the shareholders have no partnership in the management of the factory; rather, the factory owes them percentages of its value (Peninei Halakha: Pesaḥ 3:3). Vessels produced by a limited company of non-Jews require immersion, for although their ownership is of limited liability, in practice the company is in the possession of non-Jews and belongs to non-Jews.

The Rishonim and Aḥaronim did not write that a convert must immerse his vessels, and this implies that his vessels do not require immersion, but are purified with him. And so wrote the Shem Mi-Shmuel (Matot 5678) in the name of his father, the Avnei Nezer; Nezer Ha-kodesh YD 17; Tzitz Eliezer 8:20; Minḥat Asher 3:66. However, in recent generations some were in doubt about this, among them: Darkhei Teshuva 120:4, in the name of Ḥadrei De'a; Maharshag 3:48; and several rabbis of the last generation wrote to immerse them without a blessing. But in practice there is no need to be concerned about this, as emerges from all the Rishonim and Aḥaronim and from reason. Vessels belonging to state institutions require immersion with a blessing, as cited in Har Tzvi YD 109, and Tevilat Kelim 3:6 in the name of Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach.

sections.title_en: It Is Permitted to Use a Non-Jew's Vessel without Immersion
sections.body_en:
A Jew may use a non-Jew's vessel without immersion, provided that non-kosher food was not cooked in it. This is because only a vessel that a Jew bought or received as a gift from a non-Jew requires immersion; but a vessel that belongs to a non-Jew and was lent to a Jew, the Jew may use without immersion.

Some say that if a Jew received a vessel on loan from a non-Jew and the vessel remained with him for a long time, until it is clear that the non-Jew has given up hope of getting it back, the vessel has passed into the Jew's possession and he is obligated to immerse it. But in practice, if the Jew explicitly intends that the vessel remain forever in the non-Jew's possession and that he will always use it on loan, the vessel will remain in the non-Jew's ownership and will not pass into the Jew's possession against his will, and consequently it will be exempt from immersion.

When a person has a vessel that requires immersion and he is in a place with no mikveh, if there is a non-Jew there whom he trusts, he can give him the vessel as a gift and ask the non-Jew for permission to use it, for in this way the Jew may eat from it without immersion. Likewise on Shabbat, when a person needs to use vessels that he did not manage to immerse, he can give them as a gift to a trustworthy non-Jew and ask him for permission to use them (SA 120:16). It is proper after Shabbat to ask the non-Jew to give him back the vessel as a gift, and in this way he will be able to merit the mitzva and immerse it with a blessing. But if the Jew intends never to acquire it into his ownership, the vessel will remain forever in the non-Jew's ownership, and the Jew will be permitted to use it without immersion.10

notes_en.en: According to the Rif, it is permitted in a pressing situation to immerse a vessel on Shabbat, and according to the Rosh it is forbidden, because it looks like repairing a vessel (Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 22:6, note 2). In SA YD 120:16 he suggested giving the vessel as a gift to a non-Jew. The Taz 18 wrote that after Shabbat, or when a mikveh becomes available to him, he should immerse the vessel, because when the vessel becomes settled in his hand, it will become his, or will appear to be his; and since its law was not clarified by the poskim, he should immerse it without a blessing. The MB 323:35 cited this as halakha. And according to the Pri Ḥadash 120:42, after it becomes settled in his hand he should immerse it with a blessing. The basis of their view is the Gemara (Avoda Zara 75b), that if a non-Jew gave a pledge to a Jew and intended not to repay his debt and to leave the pledged vessel settled in the Jew's hand, the Jew must immerse the vessel. But if the non-Jew did not intend to leave it settled with him, they were in doubt whether the vessel requires immersion. And it was ruled that it should be immersed without a blessing (SA 120:9). Accordingly, they wished to say that since the non-Jew does not intend to take the vessel that he received as a gift from the Jew, it is like a pledge that he left settled in the Jew's hand, and it must be immersed. However, according to the Knesset Ha-gedola, the Jew may use forever a vessel that he gave to a non-Jew as a gift and received back on loan, and this also emerges from the gloss of Rabbi Akiva Eiger to se'if 1. It appears in practice that if the Jew intends never to acquire the vessel, he will not acquire it against his will, and the vessel will remain the non-Jew's and will be exempt from immersion. This is not similar to a pledge, for the purpose of a pledge is to pass into the possession of the lender, whereas here the purpose is that the vessel remain the non-Jew's. However, in order to merit the mitzva, it is proper to ask the non-Jew to transfer the vessel back to him. One can agree in advance that as soon as the Jew is able to immerse the vessel in a mikveh, the non-Jew will agree that the Jew acquire the vessel back from him, in order to fulfill the mitzva.

sections.body_en:
According to most poskim, it is forbidden to use a vessel that requires immersion for food purposes, even occasionally. However, after the fact, even if one cooked in it intentionally, the food is kosher, since the food itself did not receive a taste of anything forbidden (Rema 121:8, 16; Igrot Moshe YD 2:41).

A guest in the home of a Jew who has not immersed his vessels should not eat from his vessels. In a pressing situation, when it is not possible to use disposable vessels, and the guest's refraining from eating is liable to cause distress and insult, the guest may rely on the lenient opinion and eat from vessels that have not been immersed.

Children who have discovered that their parents' vessels are not immersed may be lenient and eat from them occasionally, in order to avoid hurting their parents. However, the children may use this permission only occasionally, so as not to spoil the meal. Afterwards they are obligated to take their parents' vessels for immersion, and if they were lazy about it, they no longer have permission to eat from them.11

Regarding the owner of a restaurant or hotel who has not immersed his vessels and regularly hosts Jews, the poskim disagree whether it is permitted to eat from his restaurant's vessels. Some say that it is permitted, because according to the basic law he is exempt from immersing them, since from his perspective they are not intended for eating but for business; and just as a merchant need not immerse the eating vessels he bought, so a restaurant or hotel owner need not immerse the eating vessels by which he earns his livelihood. And some say that it is forbidden to eat from his vessels, for since they are intended for eating by Jews, they must be immersed. Only vessels intended for sale are exempt from immersion, since they are not eaten from while they are with the merchant, but vessels intended for eating, even when one pays for this, are considered eating vessels.

In practice, restaurant owners who regularly host Jews must immerse their eating vessels with a blessing, and as long as they have not immersed them, it is forbidden to eat from them. However, in a pressing situation, when absence from the meal would cause the host distress and insult, and the foods themselves are kosher without question, it is proper to rely on the lenient opinions and participate in the meal.12

notes_en.en:
According to the Rid, Ra'avya and Rabbeinu Shmuel son of Rabbi Barukh, it is a mitzva to hurry to immerse the vessel because of holiness, but it is not forbidden to use the vessel before it has been immersed. However, according to most Rishonim, it is forbidden to use a Jew's food vessel that has not been immersed, among them: She'iltot, Rambam (Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 17:3), Riaz, Rashba and Tur. And so wrote the Rema 120:8, that it is forbidden to use a vessel that has not been immersed even occasionally. Some hold that the prohibition of using them is by Torah law (Or Zaru'a, Pri Megadim), and according to most poskim the prohibition is rabbinic (Yeshu'ot Ya'akov YD 120; BHL 323:7, s.v. "Mutar"; Beit Avi 1:116; Yabi'a Omer 2, YD 9:2). Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach explained that the prohibition is rabbinic when one cannot immerse the vessel now, but if one can and uses it without immersion, he neglects a positive Torah commandment (Tevilat Kelim 4, note 2). And according to those who hold that the entire mitzva of immersing vessels is rabbinic (above note 1), it is obvious that the prohibition of eating from them is only rabbinic.
Simply understood, a guest too is forbidden to eat from vessels that have not been immersed, and so wrote Yeḥaveh Da'at 4:44. And so one should act when it is possible to avoid the invitation or to eat from plastic or disposable vessels. However, when there is a concern of animosity, it is proper to be lenient and rely on the Rishonim who hold that it is not forbidden to eat occasionally from vessels that have not been immersed, since this is a law that according to most poskim is rabbinic (and see Da'at Kohen 227). And Responsa Beit Avi 1:116 was also lenient, because in his opinion the prohibition of eating does not apply to the guest, but only to the owner of the vessels and those who borrow or rent from him. He further added that the guest is not really considered to be using the vessels, since he could have eaten the foods from disposable vessels. Another consideration for leniency: if the food has already been placed on the plate, perhaps he is not considered to be using the plate, but only removing the food from it. And so wrote Igrot Moshe YD 3:22 regarding solid foods.
When there is a doubt whether the vessels are immersed, and asking about it may be insulting, one may be lenient and not ask because of a double doubt: a) perhaps they were immersed; b) perhaps the halakha follows those who hold that it is permitted to eat from non-immersed vessels, and perhaps the halakha is that a guest may eat from non-immersed vessels (similarly, Maharash Engel 6:56 was lenient in a case where it was doubtful whether they were immersed and doubtful whether they required immersion).

They disagreed regarding restaurants and hotels owned by Jews. Those who exempt: Darkhei Teshuva 120:70, 88; Minḥat Yitzḥak 1:44; Yeḥaveh Da'at 4:44. Those who are stringent: Levushei Mordekhai YD 83; Emek Ha-teshuva 1:121; Igrot Moshe YD 3:22. There is room to say that the Darkhei Teshuva and those who share his view were lenient with restaurants in which most of the diners were non-Jews, but when the majority are Jews, even they would agree that the vessels must be immersed with a blessing. And since the reasoning of the lenient authorities is difficult, restaurant vessels should be required to be immersed. It appears that when the restaurant owner also intends in his work to act for the sake of Heaven, to bring joy to his guests with his foods, according to all opinions he can regard his vessels as eating vessels and can immerse them with a blessing. In practice, one who holds his meal in a restaurant or hotel where there is a concern that they did not immerse the vessels must ask about this, and if they did not immerse them, he should not eat from their vessels. However, after the fact, if the host of the meal would be caused distress and insult, he may rely on those who permit eating from vessels that were not immersed.

sections.body_en:
Disposable vessels, such as an aluminum baking pan, are not considered vessels and do not require immersion. Even one who decides to use the baking pan many times does not change its nature, which is that it is intended for single use, and therefore it is exempt from immersion.

Metal cans and glass jars that are sold with the foods and drinks inside them, such as coffee in a metal can, jams in glass jars, and drinks in glass bottles, since they are usually thrown away after their contents are finished, are considered disposable vessels and need not be immersed. However, a doubt arose regarding one who wants to continue using them. Some say that they must be immersed, since by deciding to use them on a permanent basis he turned them into regular vessels, and since they were produced by a non-Jew, they must be immersed. And some are lenient and hold that since at the time of their manufacture they were intended for single use, when the Jew bought them they were exempt from immersion; and since it was the Jew who turned them into vessels by his decision to use them on a permanent basis, they are exempt from immersion. In practice, one who wishes to be lenient and not immerse them may do so, and one who wishes to be stringent should immerse them without a blessing.13

notes_en.en:
Disposable vessels do not have the status of a vessel with respect to impurity and purity, as explained in Mishna Kelim 16:5 and Rambam, Hilkhot Kelim 5:7. From this they learned that they also need not be immersed (Ḥelkat Ya'akov 3:115). And some say that they are not considered vessels at all (Igrot Moshe YD 3:23; Minḥat Yitzḥak 5:32:1; Rav Eliyahu). Some do require disposable vessels to be immersed without a blessing (Ḥazon Ovadia, Shabbat vol. 2, p. 56; Mishneh Halakhot 7:111), but the main ruling is that they are exempt from immersion, and this is the practice. At first glance it is difficult, for regarding Kiddush and washing hands it is permitted after the fact to use a disposable cup, which shows that it is considered a vessel (see Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 6, note 7; Berakhot 2:8). But the definition of a vessel does not create the obligation of immersion, as evidenced by the fact that earthenware and wooden vessels are exempt from immersion. Thus, the obligation of immersion applies only to significant vessels of metal or glass, and consequently disposable metal vessels are exempt.
Vessels that serve as packaging for food or drink and are usually thrown away after their contents are finished, as long as their contents have not been finished, according to the overwhelming majority of poskim are exempt from immersion, either because they are disposable vessels, or because this is not a use as a vessel, since one only takes out of it and does not put into it, or because one does not intend to acquire them, so as not to become obligated regarding them. The poskim disagreed regarding a case where, after their contents are finished, one decides to use them on a permanent basis. Some say that one must immerse them without a blessing (Tevilat Kelim 4:12-13; Shemirat Shabbat Ke-hilkhata 9:12; Az Nidberu 7:71). Some are lenient with glass vessels, whose obligation is rabbinic, and regarding metal vessels hold that one should not protest against those who are lenient (Igrot Moshe YD 2:40). And some are entirely lenient, since they were not considered vessels, and only the Jew, by his decision, made them vessels (Tzitz Eliezer 8:26; Or Le-Tzion 1:24; Rav Eliyahu).

sections.body_en:
There are electrical appliances intended for preparing food that come into direct contact with it, such as an electric kettle, a toaster, and a sandwich press. Seemingly they ought to be immersed, but they are liable to be damaged by the mikveh water. In practice, with simple electrical appliances the concern is remote, provided that after the immersion they are left for a long time until they are completely dry. But with delicate electrical appliances, such as appliances that have an electronic display, there is a reasonable concern that they will be damaged as a result of the immersion.

Some say that electrical appliances are exempt from immersion, because they are operated by connecting them to a wall socket to receive electricity, and the rule is that anything attached to the ground is not considered a vessel and does not receive impurity, and therefore it need not be immersed. And even if they are sometimes operated by batteries, we follow the majority of their use, which is while attached to the ground. Furthermore, electrical appliances are considered machines, and the mitzva is to immerse eating vessels and not machines. And some have added further reasons to be lenient.

In practice, one who wishes to be lenient on the basis of these opinions may do so, since their reasoning is convincing. However, since some hold that they must be immersed, when possible it is proper to take their opinion into account and immerse the appliances without a blessing, or to find another solution to exempt them from immersion.

Therefore, with an appliance that has almost no chance of being damaged, such as a simple electric kettle, it is proper to immerse it without a blessing and wait more than twenty-four hours so that it dries completely and is not damaged when it is operated.

Regarding an appliance that may be damaged, two suggestions have been raised: a) To give it to a Jewish technician, who will thoroughly dismantle the part that touches the food, until it is no longer considered a vessel, and reassemble it; in this way the vessel will be considered a vessel made by a Jew, which there is no mitzva to immerse. However, when the part that touches the food cannot be dismantled, there is no benefit in disconnecting the electric cord attached to the appliance. b) To give the appliance as a gift to a non-Jew and ask to receive it from him on loan for an unlimited time; since the appliance belongs to the non-Jew, and the Jew does not want to acquire it for himself, it may be used for an unlimited time without immersion (as explained in note 10).

All this applies to parts that are actually attached to the electrical appliance, but baking pans that are inserted into an electric oven require immersion with a blessing, because they are not considered electrical appliances, since they are not attached to the electric oven but merely placed in it, and they also sometimes serve as a vessel for serving the food baked in them. The same applies to blender blades and mixer beaters: when the part that comes into contact with the food is made of metal or glass and detaches from the electrical part, it should be immersed by itself with a blessing.14

notes_en.en: In Responsa Ḥelkat Ya'akov YD 41, 43, he was lenient regarding electrical appliances because most of their use is when they are attached to the ground and they do not receive impurity (and whatever does not receive impurity does not require immersion, as wrote Responsa Shev Ya'akov 31, Arukh Ha-shulḥan 120:39, and most Aḥaronim). And so were lenient Responsa Beit Avi 1:114, Rav Ben-Tzion Abba Shaul, Tefilla Le-Moshe 5:25, and Si'aḥ Naḥum 49:5. And Rav Ganzel (Teḥumin 27) was lenient in this for additional reasons. On the other hand, several Aḥaronim wrote that electrical appliances require immersion, among them: Minḥat Yitzḥak 2:72; Shevet Ha-levi 2:57:3; Mishneh Halakhot 9:162; Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv, Kovetz Teshuvot 1:3. And some were lenient regarding a toaster, since the bread was already ready beforehand and the toaster only improves it (Igrot Moshe YD 3:24). In my humble opinion, the view of the lenient authorities who exempt electrical appliances from immersion is more convincing, both because it operates while attached to the ground, and because it is entirely different from the vessels we were commanded to immerse, as they can be defined as a type of machine. All the more so when it cannot be immersed without being damaged, for it is inconceivable to make a vessel fit through immersion in such a way that after the immersion it will be damaged. (Furthermore, according to most poskim the prohibition of using a vessel that has not been immersed is rabbinic, as explained above in note 11.) However, since according to most poskim the obligation to immerse metal vessels is by Torah law, as explained in note 1, when possible it is proper to rule in accordance with the poskim who were stringent.
